newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE-Porous Argentine customs, a tradition getting worse.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Porous Argentine customs, a tradition getting worse.

text.p: Contraband has a long tradition in Argentina.

Between 1606 and 1625, merchants smuggled nearly 9,000 African slaves into Buenos Aires, depriving customs officials of 1.4 million silver pesos in revenue. While the slave trade is long past, the practice of smuggling through Argentina's porous entry points has exploded into gigantic proportions.
According to the government, some $10 billion worth of goods entered the capital's port illegally between 1993 and 1996, lightening state coffers by $3 billion.

Argentines, historians contend, have traditionally resorted to smuggling and tax-dodging not just for profit but also as a means of getting even with authorities they usually do not perceive as acting in their best interests.
"In the 17th and 18th centuries, people saw this kind of fraud not just as licit -- they eyed it with sympathy," author Juan Garcia wrote in his book "The Indian City."
Whatever the reason, then and now a porous port accounted for most of the illicit traffic. These days, Ezeiza international airport outside Buenos Aires comes in second.

Authorities arrested six people and launched a search for many others last month after discovering 40 tonnes of cameras, surgical instruments, perfume and other goods smuggled in from the United States. A prosecutor said he suspected the contraband had been sneaked out of Ezeiza through some of the dozens of holes recently found in the perimeter fence.
COCAINE IN THE NATIONAL BANK

In another blow last month to the customs service's battered reputation, legislators discovered 1.5 tonnes of cocaine in safe deposit boxes the service had rented in the National Bank. The drugs, with a street value of $150 million, should have been burned five days after they were seized but some had been there in bags and suitcases since 1984.
The customs administrator, Carlos Tomasetti, was later removed from his post.

A fiscal gap in the realm of $6 billion this year and an image tarnished by corruption charges against government officials have spurred President Carlos Menem's administration into action. The first spark came in September, when economic crimes judge Guillermo Tiscornia denounced what he called a "parallel customs service" bringing in billions of dollars of illegal goods through the Buenos Aires port.

Officials said corrupt customs employees helped others evade duties by marking Argentine-bound containers as being in transit to other countries and then sending them to warehouses where the goods were removed for local sale.

In early October, the customs service and the DGI tax collection agency were merged and Carlos Silvani, a widely respected economist, was brought home from an International Monetary Fund job and put in charge of cleaning up the mess.
"SCANDALOUS" LEVEL OF FRAUD SEEN

Calling the level of fraud he found "surprising and scandalous," Silvani fired all customs personnel at Ezeiza and named special administrators for all main Argentine customs points. In recent months, police have raided customs offices, supermarkets and banks, seizing goods and documents and arresting suspects.

The most senior official to be arrested to date is former customs chief Gustavo Parino, detained in mid-December on Tiscornia's orders. The judge accused Parino, who headed the customs service between 1992 and 1995, of relaxing customs controls to the point where they virtually ceased to exist.

But in a country where fraud and corruption are rampant -- the daily La Nacion declared 1996 "The Year of the Scandals" -- law enforcement can be a daunting task, especially if the accusers are under suspicion themselves.

"It is very difficult for an investigation to prosper under the circumstances," political analyst James Neilson said. "In a society where everyone believes corruption is endemic, fighting it is very hard, because everyone is accusing each other."

Such was the case with Tiscornia, who has been accused by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo of "judicial harrassment" and of being "the principal protector" of smugglers for ordering the arrest of his former customs chief. Cavallo, the architect of Argentina's return to economic growth and currency stability, contends that the case against Parino is a fabrication and calls him a "political prisoner."
Unlike other officials who are suing the former economic czar, including Interior Minister Carlos Corach, Tiscornia says it is "not worth the effort" of fighting the allegations.

Althought opinion polls show that 80 percent of Argentines believe Cavallo when he accuses officials and judges of corruption, most also think he has gone way too far without coming with solid evidence and will end up paying a high price for daring to challenge the powers that be.
"Every time he speaks he gets closer to jail," political analyst Rosendo Fraga said.
